headline_insight: No benchmark data — internal cross-portfolio or external (e.g. 60 Decibels, regional or global insurance inclusion datasets) — was supplied with the 2026 Insurance Survey dataset, so every finding in this report stands as an absolute reading of VisionFund's own clients rather than a relative one.
paragraphs: Benchmarking is the one analytical layer this report cannot deliver. The evidence pack accompanying the 2026 Insurance Survey contains no internal cross-portfolio comparison file and no external reference dataset — whether 60 Decibels client-outcome benchmarks, regional insurance uptake figures, or global inclusion baselines. In keeping with the discipline that governs the rest of this analysis, we state that gap plainly rather than filling it with approximations. Where readers encounter a percentage elsewhere in this report, it should be read as a description of what VisionFund clients said in 2026, not as evidence of over- or under-performance against a peer set.

The practical consequence is a limit on interpretation rather than a limit on usefulness. Absolute findings can still tell us whether women, clients with disabilities, and other under-served groups understand their cover, trust the claims process, and feel the product met a real risk. What they cannot tell us is whether a given result represents a sector-leading position worth protecting or a lagging one requiring urgent redesign. A figure that looks reassuring in isolation may sit well below what comparable microinsurance portfolios achieve; a figure that looks disappointing may in fact reflect a hard operating context in which VisionFund is outperforming. Without a comparator, both readings remain open, and we decline to prefer either.

This absence also constrains the GEDSI reading specifically. Gender and disability gaps are most actionable when set against a benchmark gap — the question is rarely whether a difference exists between subgroups, but whether the difference VisionFund records is wider or narrower than what similar providers record, and therefore how much of it is addressable through product and channel design. General sector context, offered here as framing and not as a finding from this survey, consistently holds that women and people with disabilities face compounding barriers to insurance access. That framing supports attention to the gaps we observe; it does not quantify them, and it should not be cited as if it did.

For programming, the recommendation is procedural and immediate. Any next iteration of the Insurance Survey should be specified from the outset with a benchmark layer attached: at minimum an internal cross-portfolio cut that allows one country's insurance clients to be read against another's, and where budget permits an external client-outcome benchmark using comparable question wording so that results are genuinely commensurable. Retrofitting comparison after fieldwork rarely works, because question phrasing and sampling frames drift. Building the comparator into the instrument is the low-cost fix, and it would convert the descriptive findings in this report into the relative, prioritised evidence that product and channel decisions actually require.
